We introduce \textbf{CaMeWM}, a causal medical world model for supported post-TACE tumor evolution and treatment planning. CaMeWM implements one intervention-to-decision loop rather than three independent prediction tasks: it first admits a queried regimen only for clinically comparable histories with empirical treatment support; it then generates a distribution of lesion-local follow-up worlds through an action-conditioned response descriptor, deterministic anchor, and residual 3D diffusion transition; and it finally maps sampled worlds to restricted mean survival time (RMST) with a response-Cox utility model. Under pre-treatment adjustment and positivity, this loop estimates a prespecified, support-restricted g-formula target; all selection and nuisance estimation are fold-local, and the induced policy is evaluated by cross-fitted, censoring-adjusted doubly robust estimation. Across 79 paired out-of-fold episodes, CaMeWM achieves 0.618 SSIM and 0.528 change-map SSIM for follow-up CT transition, while its generated-world survival pathway attains a 0.615 C-index; factual-only AIPW estimates a 9.60-week RMST gain (95\% CI 0.61--18.13) for the frozen policy. CaMeWM provides an inspectable basis for retrospective, support-restricted treatment planning.

title: Knowledge Diversion: A Novel Paradigm for Pre-training Decomposable Image Generation Models
summary: Large-scale pre-trained models have become foundational to modern machine learning, yet conventional pre-training objectives primarily optimize source-domain performance without explicitly considering downstream requirements. Consequently, transferable and task-specific knowledge remains entangled within a shared parameter space, limiting selective knowledge reuse and efficient downstream adaptation. This limitation is particularly consequential for image-generation models, which must accommodate diverse conditions and domains. To address this challenge, we introduce Knowledge Diversion (KDiv), a condition-aware pre-training paradigm for learning inherently decomposable generative models. Before pre-training, KDiv factorizes randomly initialized weights into rank-one Knowledge Units, which are organized into learngenes and tailors. During pre-training, continuous condition-aware routing consolidates knowledge shared across conditions in learngenes while directing condition-dependent variations to tailors. This structured organization enables learngenes to capture transferable generative priors and tailors to develop condition-specific expertise, allowing the resulting model to be selectively recombined for diverse downstream conditions. Extensive experiments across class-, text-, and image-conditioned generation demonstrate that KDiv consistently matches or surpasses dense baselines at comparable pre-training cost and achieves the strongest average downstream performance with a trainable parameter budget comparable to low-rank adaptation methods.

title: From Views to Worlds: Active Exploration over 3D Worlds for Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in 2D visual understanding tasks, yet the passive view-centric perception paradigm limits their capacity for 3D spatial reasoning. Such reasoning often requires actively acquiring spatial evidence beyond the currently visible views, such as camera poses and cross-view spatial relationships, to infer 3D relationships that are not explicitly represented in 2D images. However, existing methods either lack active exploration or merely provide additional views during inference, without explicitly acquiring such spatial evidence beyond 2D images. In this paper, we propose View-to-World (V2W), an active exploration framework that enables VLMs to actively explore 3D worlds and lifts VLMs from passive view-centric perception to active world-centric spatial reasoning. Given a spatial reasoning task with multi-view images, V2W first reconstructs an explicit 3D world with geometry, camera poses, and language-grounded semantics, and exposes it to VLMs through visual and linguistic interfaces. Through multi-turn interaction with these interfaces, VLMs iteratively acquire spatial evidence from the constructed 3D world, enabling active world-centric spatial reasoning. V2W can be integrated with existing VLMs in a training-free manner and can be further enhanced by optimizing the exploration policy via reinforcement learning. Experiments on spatial mental modeling benchmarks demonstrate that V2W substantially improves VLM baselines in the training-free setting and achieves state-of-the-art performance with the learned exploration policy, highlighting the importance of active exploration for spatial intelligence. Project page: \url{https://fangzhou2000.github.io/projects/v2w}.

title: MESS: Multi-Exposure Sequence Synthesis for Generalizable Image Enhancement
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code and data are available at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/MESS
summary: Despite the significant progress in image enhancement under adverse illuminations, such as low-light image enhancement, exposure correction, and backlit image enhancement, existing models show limited generalizability to different scenarios. A major bottleneck lies in the lack of large-scale and diverse training data, as these tasks typically rely on manually captured, precisely aligned image pairs that are expensive to scale up. Although synthetic data have been explored as an alternative, existing synthesis methods are limited in modeling complex adverse illumination conditions and camera imaging pipelines. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework to synthesize realistic training pairs for generalizable image enhancement in the wild. Specifically, we first derive multi-exposure sequences (MES) from high-bit RAW images by rendering them under different exposure settings through an emulated ISP pipeline. Using these RAW-derived MES as supervision, we train a diffusion-based RGB-to-MES generator to synthesize plausible exposure sequences from a single 8-bit RGB image, extending the synthesis pipeline from limited RAW collections to large-scale in-the-wild RGB data. For each source image, we randomly sample one synthesized exposure variant as the degraded input and use the original high-quality RGB image as the target. With the proposed MES Synthesis (MESS) approach, we construct a dataset of 500K training pairs and train a lightweight network, which demonstrates significantly better generalization performance than existing models across various image enhancement tasks. Code and data are available at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/MESS.

title: Geometry-Aware Interpolation for Inverse Problems
summary: Recovering missing visual information from incomplete or degraded images remains a challenging problem, particularly when spatial variations and complex image structures affect reconstruction accuracy. Although Spatial Transformer Networks (STNs) facilitate spatial feature alignment, their reliance on conventional linear or bilinear interpolation limits their ability to capture the underlying geometric characteristics of image data. Furthermore, interpolation based on a restricted set of neighbouring pixels can introduce inconsistencies in gradient propagation, potentially affecting optimisation stability. To address these limitations, we propose a Geometry-Aware Interpolation Network (GAIN), a variational autoencoder-based framework that incorporates manifold geometry into spatial transformation and image reconstruction. Rather than estimating pixel intensities solely from fixed spatial neighbours, GAIN exploits the local tangent structure of the data manifold to construct geometry-informed intensity approximations. An entropy-based regularisation mechanism further guides the estimation of spatial transformation parameters, promoting more adaptive interpolation. In addition, a convolutional normalisation strategy is introduced to regulate the magnitude of non-zero activations and improve gradient stability during training. Extensive experiments on challenging image completion and classification benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of GAIN in improving predictive accuracy while reducing computational cost compared with existing methods.

title: SuperClip Pyramid for Video Temporal Grounding
summary: With the rapid expansion of online video content, video temporal grounding has become essential for localizing moments based on user-specific queries, comprising two subtasks: moment retrieval (MR) and highlight detection (HD). While recent approaches adopt DETR-style decoders or temporal pyramid architectures, they rely on single-scale feature maps or uniformly downsampled representations, limiting their ability to capture semantic boundaries and variable-length events. In this paper, we present SuperClip Video Temporal Grounding (SCVTG) built on a multi-scale temporal hierarchy that better captures distinctive events at various granularities. SCVTG constructs a SuperClip pyramid by grouping adjacent clips into semantically coherent segments, termed SuperClips. Further, to aggregate these SuperClips having variable duration and temporal location, we introduce a temporally adaptive kernel that aggregates SuperClips through temporally conditioned weights, enabling flexible aggregation. On top of this, we design relative saliency losses to guide the model in learning inter-clip importance, enhancing its ability to distinguish relevant events. Extensive experiments show that SCVTG achieves the best performance across five video temporal grounding benchmarks with promising gains.

title: Editing Images into Reusable Layers via Compositional Edit-Prior Distillation
summary: High-quality image editing requires precise modification of target regions while preserving the content of unrelated regions. Existing editing models produce flattened outputs that limit precise local manipulation and layer reuse, while decomposition methods typically optimize layer recovery separately from instruction-driven editing. To this end, we introduce LayerEditor, a unified framework that couples instruction-guided image editing with controllable generation of reusable RGBA layers. At its core, In-Context RGB-Alpha Token Modeling jointly represents the edited canvas and an ordered sequence of RGB-Alpha layers within a single token sequence, enabling semantic edits and explicit control over individual layer content. To retain the pretrained model's editing capability during adaptation to layered outputs, we propose Compositional Edit-Prior Distillation, which transfers its editing prior to both the edited canvas and the image composed from the predicted layers. To support training and evaluation, we construct LayerEditor-100K, a large-scale paired image-editing dataset with ordered RGBA layer annotations, and introduce dedicated benchmarks for layered editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LayerEditor maintains strong editing fidelity while generating accurate RGBA layers, supporting both flexible layer-level manipulation and multi-layer decomposition.

title: CorrFlow: Self-Correcting Flow Matching
summary: Flow-matching models generate samples through iterative velocity predictions, but typically do not revisit these predictions using the intermediate representations that produced them. We introduce CorrFlow, a self-correcting flow-matching framework that reuses this information through a lightweight refiner. Under rectified-flow interpolation, the error of the one-step clean prediction equals the realized velocity residual scaled by the noise level. Motivated by this identity, the refiner learns to predict residual corrections from the base model's clean prediction, conditioning, noise level and hidden states from the same forward pass. The correction is added to the base velocity before each sampling update, so subsequent predictions are made from the corrected state. This requires no additional base-model evaluations and only one lightweight refiner evaluation per step. Our theoretical analyses establish conditions under which feature reuse outperforms raw-input affine predictors and refiner training achieves greater residual-risk reduction than continued base-model training under a matched training compute budget. Experiments on class-conditional image generation, text-to-video generation and image-to-video generation show consistent improvements over the corresponding base models, including gains in visual quality and physical consistency. Project Page: https://fogradio.github.io/corrflow-project

title: CorrCLIPv2: Harnessing Unlabeled Images for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation
comment: 25 pages, 12 figures, 12 tables. Published in International Journal of Computer Vision
summary: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation aims to classify pixels without being restricted to a fixed set of categories. Although Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) demonstrates remarkable potential for open-vocabulary recognition, its segmentation capability is impaired by noisy inter-class patch interactions. To this end, this work proposes a unified training-free object-centric framework, named CorrCLIPv2, from three complementary aspects of patch correlation, feature representation, and output regularization. Specifically, for patch correlation, we leverage class-agnostic mask generators to explicitly disentangle inter-class interactions. Moreover, we utilize spatially-coherent features from self-supervised models to compute attention scores to mitigate mask inaccuracies. Regarding feature representation, we devise a refinement mechanism to simultaneously strengthen spatial details and semantic representation. Within the output space, we unify predictions via voting in each mask to enhance spatial consistency. To mitigate contextual bias and enhance prediction accuracy of objects, we further extend the framework by incorporating a cross-image object retrieval paradigm, which incurs minimal computational overhead. We build a memory bank of CorrCLIP-enhanced features from unlabeled images and implement a regime of multi-CLIP ensemble. By aggregating semantically consistent object features across diverse contexts retrieved from the memory bank, CorrCLIPv2 mitigates context-induced interference and obtains more robust predictions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach establishes a new state-of-the-art on 10 standard benchmarks. Remarkably, it even surpasses fully supervised open-vocabulary methods across 22 multi-domain datasets. Code is available at: https://github.com/zdk258/CorrCLIP.

title: Design Anything, Design at Scale
comment: 47 pages, 25 figures, 16 tables. Project page: https://designanything.gemus.ai
summary: As multimodal resources are transformed into media outputs, agentic AI is expected to stay aligned with design intent over long horizons. Designers follow briefs specifying goals, constraints, and deliverables, with later work building on earlier decisions. Recent work reuses design experience across tasks, yet alignment among artifacts within one project remains challenging. Agents therefore need to preserve and apply this intent across domains and as projects grow. We introduce Design Anything, a graph-based harness that preserves design intent outside the model and binds deliverables to the workflow steps that produce them through an intent-execution graph. A task contract retains constraints and decisions, selected designs become explicit inputs to later generations, and a deterministic controller uses bindings and execution records to check output types and counts, identify outstanding deliverables, and guide subsequent turns. We also introduce DesignAnything-Bench, with 228 tasks across 19 design domains, including 38 project families at scales of 6, 14, and 24 artifacts. With the LLM held fixed, Design Anything satisfies 85.0% and 92.5% of the brief's factual constraints with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash High and GPT-5.6 Sol High, respectively, exceeding the strongest same-model baselines by 15.4% and 14.4%. These gains reach 25.1% and 23.0% on 24-artifact tasks. Under each model, Design Anything leads or ties in constraint satisfaction in 18 of 19 domains. Professional designers also prefer its complete deliverable sets over those of same-model baselines in a blind evaluation.

title: ATLAS: Learning to Adapt LVLM Attention for Reasoning Video Segmentation
summary: Reasoning Video Object Segmentation (RVOS) aims to localize and segment objects referred to by natural-language expressions throughout a video. Although large vision-language models (LVLMs) implicitly encode localization cues in their attention maps, these attentions are often noisy, diffuse, and scattered across layers, heads, and modalities, limiting their direct use for segmentation. Existing methods typically rely on handcrafted attention-selection heuristics or computationally expensive attention refinement. We propose ATLAS, an attention adaptation framework that learns to transform raw LVLM attentions into object-centric localization cues. ATLAS treats attentions from all layers, heads, and modalities as structured features, combining high-resolution frame-level attentions that capture spatial information with low-resolution video-level attentions that encode temporal context. A lightweight U-Net equipped with temporal attention and FiLM-based modulation fuses these complementary representations to generate coarse segmentation heatmaps, which are propagated across the video using SAM2. Extensive experiments on challenging referring and reasoning video segmentation benchmarks show that ATLAS outperforms existing frozen-backbone methods. Code and models are available at \url{https://hamidreza-136.github.io/atlas/}.

title: Video-Language Entailment for Video Similarity Estimation
summary: Comparing videos to assess their semantic similarity remains a challenging task for current Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), which are primarily trained with single-video objectives. While most prior works have focused on computing global similarity, recent studies have introduced the more challenging problem of concept-based similarity, which measures how similar two videos are with respect to specific concepts (e.g., activity, location). However, no dedicated approaches have yet leveraged LMMs to explicitly address this task. In this paper, we aim to fill this gap introducing Video Caption Entailment for video similarity estimation (VICE): a dual-branch design that leverages LMMs for cross-video reasoning. Each branch jointly processes one video and the caption of the other, measuring their alignment for a specific concept via video-language entailment. The outputs from both branches are fused to produce a final similarity score, along with a textual explanation of the model reasoning. This approach leverages the model's native single-video understanding while enabling fine-grained comparative reasoning between video and text. Experiments on ConViS-Bench and StepDiff show that VICE outperforms models that process both videos simultaneously, highlighting the promise of single-video reasoning for concept-based similarity estimation.

title: UniAVC: Unified Audio-Video Creation via Progressive Training and Asymmetric Scheduling
comment: Note: Abstract is shortened to meet arXiv's characters limitation. Page: https://hkust-longgroup.github.io/UniAVC Code: https://github.com/HKUST-LongGroup/UniAVC
summary: Unified audio-video creation requires a single model capable of text-conditioned joint synthesis, bidirectional cross-modal generation, and instruction-guided editing across both modalities. Existing methods rely heavily on paired corpora, which are scarce for joint generation and even rarer for editing. Consequently, they are spent learning single-branch generative and editing capabilities that abundant unimodal data could readily teach, rather than on the cross-modal coupling. Furthermore, prevailing systems apply a single shared noise schedule to both modalities, neglecting two critical limitations. First, due to the significant discrepancy in information density, video requires prolonged high noise to organize spatial and motion structure, whereas the sparser audio signal can settle earlier during the synthesis process, the dynamics a uniform schedule might compromise. Second, lockstep denoising leaves asymmetric workflows, such as conditioning on one modality to synthesize or edit another, untrained. We present UniAVC, which addresses both obstacles. It first trains each branch on unimodal dataset to full generative and editing competence, and subsequently dedicates paired data to exploit cross-modal correspondence. Modality-decoupled schedulers meanwhile warp the noise schedule independently from a shared timestep, while subtasks with one clean modality directly supervise asymmetric configurations. These settings respectively enable intent-aware editing, which preserves one modality intact while enlisting it to constrain the other, and post-inference self-refinement, which regenerates only an unsatisfactory branch against an accepted one. UniAVC thus spans multiple creation tasks from a single set of weights without task-specific adapters.

title: Directionally Factorized Illumination with Spherical Harmonic Rotation
summary: Many real-world capture scenarios involve an active light source rigidly attached to the camera: camera flashes for dark-environment imaging, underwater vehicle lights, and endoscopic/laparoscopic medical procedures. As the camera moves, the co-mounted light moves with it, causing the illumination direction at each surface point to change across views. Neural rendering methods (NeRF, Gaussian Splatting) encode this pose-dependent illumination as surface coloration, producing appearance inconsistencies and making it harder to recover the underlying scene. We present \textbf{DaFISH}, which can be plugged into any novel-view synthesis (NVS) pipeline such as NeRF. It factorizes per-point emitted color into surface albedo and a spherical harmonic (SH)-represented illumination factor. During training, the SH illumination is evaluated directly, enabling stable joint optimization of albedo, lighting, and geometry. \textbf{DaFISH} provides analytical generalization of illumination to arbitrary camera poses without retraining. Building on the closed-form SH-to-irradiance conversion, the training pipeline is fully differentiable from SH evaluation through volume rendering. Averaged over the held-out frames of the five scenes, \textbf{DaFISH} attains the best mean PSNR (38.91\,dB), SSIM (0.9613), and LPIPS (0.0582) among all compared methods. It improves over the strongest splatting baseline as well as the closest NeRF-based baseline, while recovering the scene consistently across views compared to prior methods.

title: SwitchSplat: Learning Discrete Object States from Casually Captured Scenes
comment: SIGGRAPH Asia 2026. 21 pages, 18 figures, 10 tables. v2 adds two sections in suppl.: A.9 Training on Native Fisheye Frames and A.10 Automatic Mask-Guided Slot Refinement
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting has made high-fidelity 3D reconstruction fast and accessible, yet existing representations assume a static world. This assumption breaks down in casual captures, where a user naturally interacts with the environment -- opening doors, toggling switches, or moving objects -- introducing discrete state changes that no current framework can model. Time-conditioned dynamic methods such as 4DGS conflate when a state was observed with what state the scene is in, limiting them to replaying seen sequences rather than composing arbitrary object configurations. We present SwitchSplat, the first 3DGS representation to address this gap via a base+slot decomposition: a shared static base captures the invariant scene, while each slot independently holds the two binary states (on/off) of one interactable object. Because the assignment of Gaussians to slots is fully differentiable, the model discovers the geometry of each state directly from video, without manual annotation. At inference, the user can freely combine slot states and render the resulting scene from any viewpoint. We validate SwitchSplat on a new casual-capture dataset and show that it outperforms static and dynamic baselines in novel-view synthesis quality, while uniquely supporting rendering of state combinations never seen during capture. Project page: https://switchsplat.github.io

title: SL-Ground: Sentence-Level Grounding for Fine-Grained Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
summary: Grounding-based open-vocabulary detectors provide a widely used framework for text-conditioned localization, with a phrase-grounding formulation that aligns object queries to individual text tokens and recovers class scores through token-to-class aggregation. We observe that this token-level scoring design becomes a bottleneck for fine-grained open-vocabulary object detection, where the target category is defined by a complete compositional description rather than by isolated tokens. Based on this observation, we propose SL-Ground, a sentence-level grounding reformulation for grounding-based open-vocabulary detection. Instead of scoring queries against fragmented token evidence, SL-Ground encodes each category description as a complete sentence-level representation and directly scores object queries against these representations. To evaluate fine-grained recognition across label granularity, we construct a multi-granularity Stanford Cars benchmark spanning vehicle type, brand, and car model. At the finest car-model granularity, SL-Ground raises AP over the token-level variant from 14.5 to 70.6 under matched training candidate sampling and to 86.0 with full-vocabulary training, while better preserving open-vocabulary capability and avoiding repeated prompt chunking. Beyond Stanford Cars, SL-Ground also improves FG-OVD performance, achieving the best average AP among compared methods. These results show that sentence-level grounding provides a more suitable scoring unit for fine-grained OVOD and offers a practical path toward fine-grained grounding-based open-vocabulary detectors.

title: Rate as a Feature, Not a Nuisance: Curriculum FiLM Training for Event-Based Graph Neural Networks
summary: An event camera emits events at a rate given by the scene motion, object texture, illumination, its own contrast thresholds, and other settings. Across the N-Caltech101 dataset, recorded by a single event camera, the event rate varies by roughly 26x. Standard event-based Graph Neural Network GNN pipelines do not make use of the variable event rate. They either normalize each event's timestamp into a fixed window or train the network to be invariant to the event rate. We argue that both choices lose information that could instead be used to improve the performance of a pipeline. Per-recording normalization is non-invertible, incurring about 6pp (percentage points) of natural-rate accuracy loss in our setting. And invariance training trades accuracy for robustness to shifts in the event rate. We instead take a different path and condition on the event rate directly. We add a per-recording log-rate scalar that modulates every stage of a PointNet++ backbone through Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), initialized to identity, so that training begins at the unmodified baseline. A two-stage curriculum (natural event rates first, then rate-augmented fine-tuning) reaches 67.2% on N-Caltech101 (+6.3pp) and 82.5% on DVS128 Gesture (+14.0pp) with an additional ~0.2M parameters. A matched-capacity control experiment shows that the gain is not from the increase in model capacity but from the rate conditioning. We will make the implementation publicly available upon acceptance of this work.

title: VTF900: A 900-Subject Visible-Thermal Face Recognition Dataset and Benchmark
comment: Accepted at IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) 2027
summary: Despite advancements in visible-thermal face recognition, where thermal probe (query) face images are matched against visible enrollment templates, existing benchmarks are currently limited by small gallery sizes (N $\approx$ 100 subjects). This limitation inhibits the ability to accurately evaluate visible-thermal facial recognition at scale and to report significant recognition performance metrics, which have better operational relevance. Therefore, we introduce VTF900, a large-scale visible-thermal face recognition benchmark with 900 subjects and paired imagery that includes expression, pose, and occlusion variations. VTF900 is designed to support large-scale (i.e., large gallery) evaluations across verification (1:1 matching) and closed-set identification (1:N matching) for visible-thermal face recognition. Furthermore, VTF900 specifically addresses the challenging combination of cross-spectral and cross-dataset analysis. In this paper, after training models on the ARL-VTF dataset, we provide benchmark analyses across convolutional (baseline), vision transformers, and domain-adaptive neural network architectures to assess how these methods scale. At full gallery scale (N = 900), transformer models achieve strong discriminative performance under frontal conditions (e.g., ViT-B: 97.68% AUC, 51.10% TAR@1%FAR), while domain-adaptive methods such as DPIT-ResNet50 demonstrate greater robustness under off-pose conditions (94.68%AUC, 36.08% TAR@1%FAR). Our results show that high AUC at small scale does not translate to reliable performance at deployment scale, and that pose variation significantly amplifies performance degradation. VTF900 exposes these limitations, enabling more rigorous evaluation of cross-spectral face recognition systems.

title: PCHMR: Empowering and Benchmarking Human Mesh Recovery in Privacy-Constrained Real-World Settings
summary: Fine-tuning directly on user-side data is an effective way to improve the performance of widely adopted data-driven human mesh recovery (HMR) models. However, doing so for existing HMR methods often assumes aggregating user-side data from real-world HMR-deployed devices to a central training server, posing a significant privacy risk as sensitive human images are transmitted. How can human mesh recovery be evaluated and improved in privacy-constrained real-world settings? We study this question through a benchmark in which state-of-the-art HMR models are trained with federated learning and a secure-aggregation variant, neither of which centralizes raw images, and evaluated across a wide range of client-scale and data-heterogeneity settings. We document that common HMR training pipelines are built around centralized data access and quantify how representative HMR backbones behave when that assumption is removed. Furthermore, to study the data bottleneck of privacy-constrained HMR training, we propose DePoser, a local annotation and fine-tuning pipeline enhanced with depth foundation models, with which collaboratively trained HMR models can be locally tailored to the end user's distribution. On in-the-wild data, fine-tuning on DePoser annotations improves personalization accuracy, measured against DePoser-generated pseudo-ground truth. This benchmark aims to support future work on privacy-constrained HMR models and their real-world deployment and evaluation.

title: Arbitrary-Scale Anisotropic 3D MRI Super-Resolution with Gaussian Prototypes
summary: Reducing MRI acquisition time improves patient comfort, reduces motion artefacts, and increases scanner throughput. Clinical protocols often shorten acquisitions by sacrificing spatial resolution, particularly along the slice axis. Super-resolution can recover higher-resolution images, but existing methods are typically specialised to one scale or acquisition geometry, limiting their use across heterogeneous clinical protocols. We present GSMR3D, a continuous volumetric model that reconstructs arbitrary isotropic and anisotropic resolutions with a single checkpoint per MRI contrast. It combines a learned dictionary of anisotropic 3D Gaussian prototypes with scale-conditioned frequency encoding and an exact measurement-consistency projection, keeping reconstructions consistent with the acquired low-resolution data. We train separate models on 3,731 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted and 30,254 T1-weighted brain MRI volumes from clinical and population-based cohorts. We evaluate GSMR3D against geometry-specific specialists for isotropic, in-plane, and through-plane super-resolution using reconstruction quality and downstream tasks: brain tumour segmentation, brain-metastasis detection, and brain parcellation. GSMR3D outperforms specialists at isotropic $2\times$ and achieves better LPIPS, DISTS, and FID across all geometries, although specialists retain higher PSNR in anisotropic settings. It more faithfully preserves glioma segmentations across all geometries, achieves the highest lesion sensitivity on an independent brain-metastasis cohort, and the highest brain-parcellation agreement for isotropic and in-plane reconstruction. Reconstruction takes about 6s per volume, adding little overhead relative to acquisition-time savings. GSMR3D offers a flexible approach to MRI scan-time reduction with one model per contrast across geometries while preserving information relevant to downstream tasks.

title: SpriteStage: Long Horizon Animation Generation via Progressive Scene Programming and Replay
summary: Video generation models synthesize visual sequences from text and image inputs. Extending video generation to long animations requires actions, dialogue, camera coverage, and narrative developments to remain coordinated across scenes. Executable scene programs make these decisions available for inspection. Constructing an entire story before observing its execution can leave later scenes dependent on unrealized events. We present SpriteStage, a progressive scene programming framework that builds animation through iterative enactment and engine reorchestration. Iterative enactment generates each scene from an accepted world checkpoint and narrative snapshot, executes it on a shared spatial stage, and uses runtime and visual feedback to revise the relevant actions or story beats. The accepted outcome becomes the starting state for the next scene. Engine reorchestration maps the resulting draft to production assets and engine capabilities while retaining its events, geometry, and timing. Inspection of the assembled sequence and frozen replay carry the accepted performance into the final video. Three complete animations, ranging from approximately 9.9 to 14.3 minutes, demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in producing extended narratives through scene programming and engine execution.

title: Goal Images Are Control Targets: Spatially-Grounded Goal-Image Synthesis for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Goal-conditioned manipulation policies are steered by a goal image, a picture of the desired post-manipulation scene synthesized from the current observation and a language instruction. The prevailing assumption is that better image-editing quality yields better goals, so goal generators are built and compared using general image-editing metrics. We show this assumption is false. Across two independent goal-conditioned policies on CALVIN, the image editors that top aggregate editing-quality leaderboards (Gemini 3 Pro Image and GPT Image 1.5) produce worse control targets than our proposed far smaller finetuned open models, and the gap widens sharply for the multi-step (long-horizon) tasks robots actually face. A per-dimension analysis explains why. Downstream policy success is governed almost entirely by manipulation adherence (selecting the right object and the right final state; Spearman $ρ\approx 0.9$ with success), while photorealism and aesthetic fidelity, precisely where large proprietary editors excel, are uncorrelated with success ($ρ\approx 0$). This dissociation holds on both CALVIN and the real-world-aligned SIMPLER-Bridge benchmark. We then present SGE-Goal, a spatially-grounded decomposed editing framework that predicts initial and final 2D edit-region masks before goal-image synthesis. SGE-Goal turns open base models (FLUX.1 Kontext, FLUX.2 klein) into the strongest goal generators we evaluate on CALVIN, and second only to Gemini 3 Pro Image on SIMPLER-Bridge. Base models fine-tuned with SGE-Goal also hold up under chaining far better than the best proprietary editor, sustaining roughly seven times the success rate at the longest (five-step) chains. We release code, datasets, checkpoints, and a human-aligned diagnostic evaluator. Our results argue that goal generators must be selected by downstream utility, not by editing-quality leaderboards.

title: Multi-Speed Field Evaluation of a Semi-Autonomous Precision Sprayer for Weed Control in Vegetable Crops
summary: Machine vision-guided precision spraying is promising for sustainable vegetable production by enabling site-specific weed targeting, reducing herbicide application while protecting crop yield and quality. However, the effects of operating speed of sprayer systems on the integrated detection-tracking-actuation pipeline remain insufficiently characterized under field conditions. This study evaluated a semi-autonomous, tractor-based spraying system for targeted weed control in radish and quantified performance across three operating speeds. A five-season dataset comprising 10,599 images and 84,311 annotated instances across seven classes was curated for model development. A YOLOv11-medium model was integrated with ByteTrack tracking and a customized 12-nozzle sprayer on a semi-autonomous electric tractor. Field trials were conducted at 0.13, 0.27, and 0.45 m/s (i.e., 0.3, 0.6, and 1.0 mph) to characterize speed-dependent changes in weed detection, targeting, actuation, and crop damage. At the lowest speed of 0.13 m/s, the system achieved 94.6% mAP@50 and 93.2% recall for weed and crop detection. However, increasing platform speed substantially reduced system performance, with weed hit rate declining from 78.3% to 35.0% and crop contact rates increasing from 20.1% to 28.7%. Consequently, the system did not meet predefined commercial-viability thresholds. These results demonstrate that practical deployment requires improvements beyond weed detection alone, particularly coordinated improvements in motion-robust plant perception, spray-timing compensation, and crop-adjacent actuation precision. The identified performance bottlenecks provide specific engineering targets for advancing vision-guided precision spraying toward practical, high-speed vegetable weed management. The software programs developed in this study have been made publicly available to support future precision weeding research.

title: Predicting Individual Differences in Lipreading From Eye-Tracking and Pupillometry During Silent Visual Speech
comment: Submitted to the Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research. 5 figures, 2 tables
summary: Lipreading ability varies widely, including among people who are hard of hearing. Although mouth-directed attention is linked to speechreading outcomes, it remains unclear how much lipreading skill can be inferred from viewing behavior and which signals carry this information. We examine whether individual differences in lipreading ability are reflected in viewing behavior during silent speech and quantify the contributions of gaze dynamics, pupil-linked signals, and spatial viewing allocation. We introduce the Lipreading Perception Study (LiPS) dataset and a tracker-independent preprocessing pipeline that synchronizes SR Research EyeLink gaze and pupil recordings with the stimuli. Twenty-four adults (age 32 $\pm$ 10 years) completed a four-alternative forced-choice silent lipreading task. An extreme-groups protocol yielded 18 participants labeled as stronger or weaker lipreaders. Each participant-trial included four aligned views: lip-region images, frame-level gaze, pupil summaries, and spatial viewing proportions. A four-branch neural network with cross-modal attention predicted labels using participant-disjoint splits and systematic ablations. The full model reached accuracy 0.680 $\pm$ 0.040 across five folds, outperforming naive fusion baselines in accuracy. The pupil and viewing-summary branch was most informative: removing it caused the largest degradation (0.618 accuracy, 0.623 AUC), while it alone achieved 0.675 accuracy. The lip-image stream contributed little to participant-level discrimination. Individual differences in lipreading are reflected in pupil-linked and frame-level gaze signals rather than in how much time a viewer spends looking at the mouth. Synchronized gaze and pupillary measures may provide objective markers of visual speech perception, warranting investigation in larger, clinically diverse populations. LiPS provides a resource for extending this work.

title: Stable Signer V3: 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting Is All You Need for Sign Language Production
summary: We present Stable Signer V3, an interactive high-resolution sign language avatar system built on 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting. It addresses three limitations of existing avatars: restricted facial expression, inaccurate identity-specific body deformation, and loss of fine appearance details. Shared Face Primitive Splatting adds transferable superquadric primitives for richer expression control; Test-Time Body Primitive Splatting learns an identity-specific virtual muscle layer for more faithful motion; and Test-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution uses TunnelingNet to recover identity-specific high-resolution details. Both test-time modules are optimized once per signer identity; inference then runs entirely from the stored identity parameters. Together, they reduce facial geometry error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2% on held-out evaluations, while retaining interactive streaming.

title: Meta Inverse Prompting for Video Generative Models
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Project page: https://ueriniuno.github.io/mvip-page/ Code: https://github.com/ueriniuno/MVIP
summary: Recent advances in video generative models have enabled flexible conditional generation and editing pipelines, such as text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-guided synthesis. However, these workflows are inherently one-directional, mapping conditions to videos without providing a mechanism to invert this process. In complex media production settings, the ability to recover controllable textual conditions from a given video is highly desirable, yet remains underexplored. While inverse prompting has been studied for image generation, directly extending these approaches to video is challenging due to the need to capture temporal dynamics beyond static appearance, as well as the substantial computational cost of per-video optimization. In this work, we propose the first practical framework for efficient video inverse prompting. Specifically, we formulate inverse prompting as a meta-learning problem and introduce Meta Video Inverse Prompting (MVIP), which learns a meta-prompt optimized over temporal dimensions to enable fast and effective prompt inference. Our approach amortizes the inversion process, eliminating the need for costly iterative optimization at test time. Experimental results demonstrate that MVIP recovers higher-quality inverse prompts with significantly improved reconstruction fidelity compared to image-based inversion and iterative captioning baselines, while achieving substantial gains in efficiency. Code and video results are available at https://ueriniuno.github.io/mvip-page/.

title: Visual Sufficiency Landscapes: Understanding Query-Conditioned Reliability in Visual Token Pruning
summary: Different visual token pruning strategies retain different subsets while maintaining similar task performance. This motivates a combinatorial question: how many visual subsets can preserve model behavior, and how does their abundance depend on the query? We introduce visual sufficiency landscapes to characterize this abundance. At a fixed layer and budget, visual sufficiency probability is the fraction of uniformly sampled subsets that jointly preserve the dense model's answer, reference-answer likelihood, and output distribution. Independent sampling replicates separate input variation from estimation noise. Across Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2-8B, and LLaVA-v1.5-7B, differences between inputs on GQA and TextVQA exceed replication error, and different questions about the same GQA image produce distinct landscapes. Sufficiency probability also improves failure prediction for full pruning methods. On LLaVA, adding this probability increases AUC by 0.1151 for FastV, 0.0683 for VisionZip, and 0.1401 for SparseVLM, while reducing log loss and Brier score. Several architecture-adapted configurations on the other two models reproduce these gains. Under controlled selection rules, predictors trained on the original images reduce log loss on new images by 9.0%, 13.0%, and 14.1%, respectively. These results establish successful-subset abundance as a measurable dimension of local prunability and connect it to the identification of high-risk pruning conditions.

title: MultiAltitudeSR: Multi-Altitude Agricultural UAV Image Super-Resolution via Physical Ground Sampling Distance Conditioning
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) enable high-throughput platforms for crop monitoring but face a fundamental trade-off between flight altitude and image spatial resolution. Many existing super-resolution (SR) methods for UAV imagery rely on oversimplified synthetic degradation models and are restricted to fixed integer upsampling scales, limiting their ability to handle real-world degradations and varying flight altitudes. This study proposes MultiAltitudeSR, a framework that conditions feature modulation and reconstruction on source and target ground sampling distances (GSDs). MultiAltitudeSR trained jointly on real UAV images at altitudes of 10 to 70 m above ground level supports all 21 source-to-target altitude pairs without pair-specific fine-tuning, covering scale factors ranging from 1.18$\times$ to 6.03$\times$. The framework can be extended to additional source-target GSD combinations by incorporating corresponding image pairs into training. On the 20-to-10 m pair, the model achieved competitive perceptual performance compared with pair-specific baselines, with LPIPS of 0.2236, DISTS of 0.2431, and NIQE of 8.9020. Experiments using the same architecture demonstrated the value of acquiring real-world multi-altitude UAV image pairs for SR training, with real-pair training achieving better average reconstruction performance across the 21 altitude pairs than training with the tested synthetic degradation pipeline. Downstream zero-shot segmentation case studies illustrated task-dependent benefits of super-resolved imagery for crop monitoring, suggesting potential UAV flight-time savings through image acquisition at higher altitudes.

title: ReTrace: Visual Backtracking for Efficient Multimodal Large Language Models
comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026, forthcoming
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) encode images into dense visual token sequences, creating substantial attention and KV-cache overhead. Existing visual token compression methods reduce this cost by pruning low-saliency tokens in shallow layers, but this practice couples temporary computational deactivation with irreversible information deletion. We show that this coupling breaks an intrinsic inference pattern in MLLMs. Through layer-wise attention analysis, we identify \textbf{Visual Backtracking}: visual pivots remain spatially stable, yet in middle layers they actively retrieve context from tokens that appeared unimportant earlier. Thus, early low-saliency tokens can be inactive for computation while still being useful for later reasoning. Motivated by this finding, we propose \textbf{ReTrace}, a backtracking-aware compression framework that introduces a dormant token state. ReTrace caches non-pivot tokens outside expensive layer-wise computation, restores them during the backtracking window, and prunes only after their information has been absorbed. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3 demonstrate nearly 90\% reductions in FLOPs and KV cache, a 2.83$\times$ prefilling speedup, and strong performance retention across complex vision-language benchmarks.

title: FineSplat: Fine Patches, Local Groups, Detailed Splats
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) promises instant scene reconstruction with high-quality novel-view synthesis. Yet, fine-grained geometry and appearance remain difficult to recover, motivating us to revisit how feed-forward models represent, aggregate, and refine detailed visual information. We introduce FineSplat, a feed-forward 3DGS framework built around fine-grained image patches. Since global multi-view attention becomes prohibitively expensive at such high token resolutions, we develop a dual-grouping strategy that combines two complementary forms of locality: view-wise grouping enables efficient interaction among neighboring views, while 3D spatial grouping reconnects geometrically related tokens that may never have interacted under view-wise grouping by lifting them into the 3D scene space. We further leverage reconstruction error as direct feedback, providing an explicit rendering-based signal to recover fine-grained structures and appearance, thereby overcoming the limitations of one-pass feed-forward prediction. Finally, a compact Gaussian generation scheme preserves the benefits of fine-grained features without unnecessarily increasing the number of primitives. Together, these designs enable FineSplat to recover richer geometry and appearance while remaining efficient and compact, achieving state-of-the-art results by a substantial margin, under the same or smaller Gaussian budgets than existing methods.

title: IECLA: Interpretable Emotion Contribution Learning for Affective Image Editing
comment: 31 pages, 10 figures, 24 tables; under review at ICLR 2027
summary: Affective image editing (AIE) aims to evoke a target emotion while preserving the content and structure of a source image. Existing methods improve emotional expression or visual fidelity, but the target emotion alone does not reveal which source regions should be changed and which should remain intact, especially in complex scenes. We introduce Interpretable Emotion Contribution Learning for Affective Image Editing (IECLA), a framework that separates source-emotion attribution from target-aware editing. IECLA constructs signed object-level supervision through counterfactual interventions and trains a context-conditioned contribution predictor to localize evidence that supports or opposes the source emotion. At inference, an image-level evaluator estimates the source emotion directly from the input, while the predictor identifies editable and preservation evidence without repeated interventions. A target-aware editing agent then translates this evidence and the desired emotion into localized, content-aware operations for existing editors. Extensive evaluations show that IECLA predicts counterfactual contributions more faithfully on both in-domain and cross-dataset tests, while external VLM and independent human references support the quality of its localized evidence. Across six editing backbones, IECLA consistently strengthens target-emotion expression while preserving image content and structure, and user studies further show improved perceived target expression and naturalness.

title: PRET is a few-shot system for pan-cancer recognition without example training
summary: Pathological examination stands as the cornerstone in cancer diagnosis, impacting millions worldwide annually. With the shortage of pathologists globally, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged rapidly to automate the diagnostics process. However, conventional AI models require substantial labeled data for each disease, posing huge challenges in scalability and practicality. Therefore, we introduce PRET (pan-cancer recognition without examples training), a few-shot system to achieve flexible, scalable, and effective cancer recognition across diverse organs, hospitals and tasks without training. Evaluated on 23 international benchmarks comprising 4,484 whole-slide images, our method outperforms existing approaches across 20 tasks, achieving over 97% area under the curve on 15 benchmarks with a maximum improvement of 36.76%. Notably, PRET delivers clinical-grade diagnostic performance in lymph node metastasis detection using only eight slide examples, outperforming 11 pathologists. By offering a flexible and cost-effective solution for pan-cancer recognition, PRET paves the way for accessible and equitable AI-based pathology systems, particularly benefiting minority populations and underserved regions.

title: MoWE: Spatially Adaptive Mixture-of-Wavelet-Experts Pooling for Ultrasound Lesion Segmentation
summary: We present Mixture-of-Wavelet-Experts (MoWE), a spatially adaptive routing mechanism that replaces max-pooling and strided convolutions in U-Net architectures for ultrasound lesion segmentation. Standard pooling operations suppress high-frequency spatial details, including potential boundary cues in speckled regions. Recent frequency-domain methods preserve some of these details, but a single wavelet family applies the same spectral bias across the image. MoWE instead uses a context-aware router to assign local regions to fixed wavelet families according to local texture and global feature context. The decoder reuses the encoder's spatial routing maps during the inverse transform. Learnable channel-wise gates rescale the high-frequency subbands before reconstruction. We evaluate MoWE with U-Net on four ultrasound lesion benchmarks (BUSI, TN3K, UDIAT, BUS-UCLM) and one cardiac dataset (CAMUS), and with nnU-Net on BUSI. On BUSI, MoWE improves U-Net Dice from 72.59\% to 74.55\% and reduces HD95 from 47.01 to 43.49\,px. With nnU-Net, MoWE improves Dice from 80.18\% to 81.97\% and reduces ASSD from 20.07 to 17.25\,px. On U-Net, MoWE reduces trainable parameters by 6.4\%.

title: MoCKEFA: Model-Conditioned Keyframe Extraction and Fair Attribution for Video Model Explanation
summary: We show that a video can be represented with just a few keyframes without sacrificing a given model's belief about the video. Our method is the first of its kind that extracts these keyframes conditioned on the model's prediction, which is massively helpful for building explainable video models. We then fairly distribute the importance of the video to the model among the keyframes with game theoretically fair Shapley values. Through qualitative and quantitative experiments, we show that keyframe attribution is superior to the traditional frame attribution. Further, we conduct preliminary exploration on highlighting the important changes among the frames by looking at the differences between adjacent keyframes.

title: Sufficient Frame Subsets for Video Understanding
summary: Understanding when during a video a model makes its critical observations is essential for interpreting video-understanding systems. However, existing attribution methods often spread evidence diffusely across near-duplicate frames. We introduce Sufficient Frame Subsets: compact sets of frames in which all other frames are masked, yet each subset independently preserves the model's prediction. We evaluate our method on two complementary benchmarks, UCF101 and Something-Something v2, using both CNN- and transformer-based architectures. Our results show that the proposed algorithm identifies highly compact and effective frame subsets for explaining model decisions. We also find that models capable of relying on a greater number of sufficient frame subsets tend to perform better, possibly because they are more robust, consistent with prior research. Finally, the extracted frame subsets help us analyze model failure cases, reveal which aspects of a video the model has learned to emphasize, and identify opportunities for improving future training procedures.

title: Think Visually Across Space and Time: Grounded Reasoning for Video Segmentation
summary: Video Reasoning Segmentation (VRS) requires a model to identify an implicitly described target and predict its pixel-level mask trajectory, while resolving the spatial relations and temporal events that determine the answer. Text-only Chain-of-Thought (CoT) can explain a target choice without making the underlying visual references explicit, leaving a \emph{video reference gap} between linguistic inference and the evidence distributed across frames. We introduce \textbf{Temporal Chain of Video Primitives (TCoVP)}, a spatiotemporally grounded form of Video CoT that organizes query-relevant observations into a chronological reasoning chain. Each primitive associates an entity reference with temporal support and timestamped spatial evidence, and the chain interleaves these references with language to guide reasoning about which entity is relevant, when the queried event holds, and where its evidence appears. The selected target primitives then provide box prompts and temporal support for video mask prediction. We construct TCoVP-SFT-15k and TCoVP-RL-13k to learn this representation through supervised fine-tuning and chain-aligned reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments across five VRS benchmarks and three model backbones demonstrate the strong performance of TCoVP, highlighting the effectiveness of organizing spatial and temporal evidence within the reasoning process. All models and code will be publicly released. Project page: \url{https://victor-wjw.github.io/TCoVP/}

title: From Zero to OCR: A Data-Centric Framework for Unsupported Low-Resource Scripts
summary: Optical character recognition (OCR) remains inaccessible to many low-resource scripts because annotated document images are unavailable and synthetic training data can fail to preserve script-specific visual structure. We present a data-centric framework that builds end-to-end OCR for such scripts from only an unannotated text corpus and digital fonts, without manually annotating a single training image. A synthetic data engine renders word, line and page images with correct complex-script shaping and automatically derived labels; a YOLOv8 word detector and a convolutional recurrent recognizer trained with connectionist temporal classification learn from these images; and a stage-gate evaluation protocol isolates recognition error before detection is introduced. We demonstrate the framework on Kashmiri, a Perso-Arabic Nastaliq script with approximately 6.8 million speakers that none of six widely used OCR engines supports. Three line-level recognizers, including one transferred from Arabic, stalled between 41% and 79% character error rate (CER), motivating a word-level formulation; subsequent improvements came primarily from rendering fidelity, diacritic-preserving crop margins and tuned non-maximum suppression. The resulting system achieves 0.39% CER on held-out words, 10.0% on synthetic pages and 13.5% on browser-rendered digital pages, and establishes reference results of 18.45% on typeset book pages and 49.8% on degraded historical documents. We publicly release the trained models, the inference code and a synthetic dataset of 285,864 Kashmiri text-line images, and we describe a step-by-step procedure for building OCR for other unsupported scripts.

title: LC-TSRNet: A Land-Cover-Guided Two-Stage Network for Annual MODIS Surface Reflectance Time Series Reconstruction
summary: MODIS surface reflectance (SR) products often suffer from data gaps due to cloud contamination and sensor malfunctions, limiting their applications in long-term and large-scale studies. Most existing methods rely on cloud-free observations from optical time series or introduce SAR time series as auxiliary information. However, due to the coarse spatial resolution of MODIS, cloud-free reference images are difficult to obtain, and SAR imagery is not well matched to the spatial resolution of MODIS, making it difficult to provide effective prior constraints. To address these issues, this study proposes LC-TSRNet for seamless reconstruction of annual MODIS SR products. In the first stage, an annual land cover map is introduced as prior knowledge, and CSPM is designed by leveraging the spectral similarity within identical land cover types, thereby providing prior spectral constraints for missing regions. In the second stage, to address large-area, persistent, and overlapping gaps in MODIS imagery, SMRM is designed to adaptively exploit and integrate multi-scale spatiotemporal contextual information. Meanwhile, to address the limited collaborative utilization of spatio-temporal-spectral information, 3DAM is designed to impose cross-dimensional joint constraints. Considering the lack of publicly available MODIS sample datasets, this study constructs the AIRMOD-TSR dataset. Extensive experimental results show that LC-TSRNet outperforms the comparison methods and achieves better reconstruction accuracy and spectral fidelity. Under the spatially adjacent scenario, LC-TSRNet improves PSNR by 0.56 dB and reduces SAM by 0.13°. The vegetation monitoring application further verifies the practical value of the reconstructed SR time series.

title: HullProbe: Measuring Interventional Part Reliance in Maritime Vessel Classifiers
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027 (Evaluation & Dataset Track). 20 pages including supplementary material, 12 figures, 15 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/fossil-ai/HullProbe
summary: Recognizing a vessel's type from an image supports maritime surveillance and sanctions monitoring, but a classifier can reach high accuracy by leaning on the generic hull instead of the more distinctive superstructure, and is then fooled when a vessel is re-hulled or occluded. De-biasing methods claim to remove such reliance, yet the field certifies them with worst-group accuracy, a proxy that needs group labels and only infers reliance from accuracy. We measure the reliance directly. HullProbe swaps a registered anatomical part of a vessel for another instance's and reads how much that part drives the decision, using a same-class swap to control for compositing artifacts. Because a surface vessel is a hull and a superstructure arranged along one axis, its parts form a 2x3 grid whose 2^6 = 64 swaps we evaluate exhaustively, and a single Walsh transform returns each part's interventional influence and its interaction spectrum. On planted shortcuts, where the true reliance is known, the measure tracks worst-group accuracy (r = -0.94 over 45 configurations), and replacing its learned segmenter with human annotations changes the hull-share by less than the audit's resolution. On the 26 vessel types of MARVEL, the classifier places about 46% of its corrected sensitivity on the generic hull yet follows the superstructure when the two conflict, and the group-label-free de-biasers available there do not detectably reduce the hull's share. The findings hold across three architectures and a second maritime dataset, and the method extends to fine-grained vehicle recognition on Stanford Cars.

title: Reflection-Guided Dynamics Rectification for Text-to-Image Generation
comment: This paper is 20 pages long, including the appendices, and contains 10 figures. Interactive demos, code, and the dataset are available on the project page: https://mair-lab-hust.github.io/RGDR/
summary: Fine-grained rectification of existing generations under a limited additional budget remains a key problem in test-time optimization (TTO) for image generation. As for prior approaches, they could identify residual errors, but could not directly ensure that the model acts on the feedback during reasoning. Such errors stem from multiple sources, such as the initial noise or text prompt, and ultimately induce an execution gap of failing to handle potential deviations along the trajectory generating. However, classic models generally cannot remedy this gap. To narrow it, we propose Reflection-Guided Dynamics Rectification (RGDR), which turns reflections on completed outputs into corrective interventions on the process of sampling dynamics at the trajectory level. Specifically, RGDR could impact every sampling step by adapting to instantaneous intervention. Moreover, RGDR generates flexible candidates while adjudicating between them and the reference. As experiments show, rectification from RGDR starts from the existing base trajectory and reflection, and RGDR is substantially more effective than former trajectory exploration. Under matched budgets for additional image generation, RGDR's gain in the cross-model average final checklist score over the reference is $1.51\times$ that of TIR prompt refinement and $1.81\times$ that of Dynamic CFG.

title: Image Dehazing as In-Context Tabular Inference
summary: Image dehazing is traditionally addressed through handcrafted physical priors or task-specific deep learning models, often requiring carefully designed architectures or extensive model training. Recent advances in tabular foundation models (TFMs), however, offer an alternative learning paradigm in which continuous relationships can be inferred directly from contextual examples without task-specific model training. Motivated by this capability, this paper investigates whether single-image dehazing can be effectively reformulated as an in-context tabular regression problem and introduces DehazeTab, a framework that estimates atmospheric transmission from structured image-patch representations. Specifically, overlapping patches extracted from hazy images are transformed into tabular samples using handcrafted haze-related descriptors, pretrained visual embeddings, or their hybrid combinations, while corresponding transmission patches are summarized as scalar regression targets. A pretrained TFM then performs in-context regression using labeled reference patches to predict transmission values for unseen images without any further fine-tuning. These predictions are spatially aggregated into a transmission map, refined through guided filtering, and incorporated into the atmospheric scattering model to recover haze-free images. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate competitive restoration performance and reveal that physically motivated handcrafted features can outperform pretrained visual embeddings, while hybrid representations offer complementary benefits. Further analyses examine the effects of feature representations, patch selection, and contextual reference configurations on restoration quality. Beyond image dehazing, the findings highlight the potential of TFMs as an alternative paradigm for addressing low-level vision tasks through structured and in-context inference.

title: PLANE: Plug-and-Play Fine-Grained Visual Experts for Hallucination Mitigation in Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) commonly suffer from hallucinations, which appear as fabricating non-existent objects or outputting incorrect attributes and spatial relationships in images. Previous works empirically indicate that CLIP-style vision encoders tend to focus on primary objects while ignoring image details, which is one of the causes of hallucinations. To address this issue, we propose plug-and-play fine-grained visual experts (PLANE) comprising two components: LoRA visual experts operating on CLIP for multi-aspect image encoding, and an instruction-aware gate network for adaptive image feature fusion. During training, we construct a fine-grained image-caption pairs dataset, where images are described from three aspects: objects, attributes, and relations between objects. Image-caption pairs from different aspects are used to train the three fine-grained LoRA experts respectively. Aiming at comprehensively evaluate our method's capabilities, we manually annotate a fine-grained hallucination evaluation benchmark for LVLMs which is GPT4-independent during evaluation phase (GIFT). We conduct experiments both on popular hallucination evaluation benchmarks and GIFT. The results show that our method effectively reduces hallucinations across models of different types and sizes while introducing minimal inference latency. Compared to advanced baselines, our model also demonstrates superior performance.

title: Deep Auxiliary Learning via Bilevel Feature Optimization for Label-Efficient Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Auxiliary learning (AL), which can improve the performance of a primary task by leveraging related auxiliary tasks, is commonly regarded as a special case of multi-task learning. Existing AL approaches typically require manually annotated auxiliary labels, increasing annotation costs, particularly in medical imaging where expert labeling is expensive. In this work, we investigate whether segmentation performance can be improved using auxiliary tasks whose labels are automatically derived from existing segmentation annotations, requiring no additional manual labeling. To address this, we propose a novel auxiliary learning framework, formulated as a bilevel optimization problem. Our method enables effective knowledge transfer between tasks via a feature communication module, enhancing the primary segmentation task. We evaluate the method on three medical image segmentation benchmarks under limited-label settings. The results demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, achieving superior label efficiency. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/FupingWu90/ALBO.

title: Map2Vid: Embodied Navigation Video Generation with Human-Friendly Motion Control
summary: Controllable video generation has recently achieved impressive visual quality, yet existing control paradigms remain poorly suited to embodied navigation. Text prompts are spatially ambiguous, while camera-trajectory control relies on low-level motion specifications that are unintuitive for human users and difficult to manipulate. In this work, we introduce Map2Vid, a novel task that reformulates embodied navigation video generation as a BEV-map-to-video synthesis problem, together with a large-scale benchmark for systematic evaluation. By using BEV maps, which provide a visual representation of global scene layout and intended navigation routes, Map2Vid enables human-friendly navigation video generation. To support this task, we construct a dedicated dataset with over 100K navigation sequences across 61 indoor scenes, each paired with egocentric videos, BEV maps, camera trajectories and language instructions. We further develop a unified framework that integrates multiple control signals, together with a curriculum training strategy that progressively weakens non-map inputs, enabling flexible inference under both full conditioning and map-only input. Extensive experiments across multiple foundation generation models demonstrate that controllable navigation video generation via BEV map is a viable and promising direction.

title: Evaluating Cloud and Self-Hosted OCR Systems for Arabic, English, and French Documents: Bounding Box Detection, Text Recognition, and Mathematical Expression Recognition
summary: Choosing an OCR system for a multilingual archive requires balancing accuracy against deployment constraints. This study compares cloud and self-hosted systems on three tasks: bounding box detection on 48 Arabic, English, and French pages, text recognition on 315 pages across nine document types, and mathematical expression recognition on 83 English and Arabic samples. Detection was assessed by page-level visual grades, text by character error rate (CER) against a Gemini-generated reference transcription, and mathematics by scores against known answers. Main estimates are accompanied by 95% intervals and paired comparisons. Google Document AI and Surya produced Good line boxes on 47 of 48 (98%) and 46 of 48 (96%) pages. Datalab, Azure Document Intelligence, and Document AI had mean CERs of 0.145-0.152, with no difference detected in unadjusted paired comparisons. Surya had the lowest mean CER among self-hosted systems (0.199). No mathematical test had a statistically clear leader. Strict checks showed that near-perfect page scores could conceal a replaced Arabic variable or Eastern Arabic digits rewritten in Western form. Reliable evaluation therefore requires uncertainty estimates, structural checks, and notation-specific tests in addition to aggregate recognition scores.

title: GeoV2V: Geometry-Grounded Video Diffusion Model for Driving Scene Generation
comment: Published at ECCV 2026. Author accepted manuscript. Project page: https://xiyuche.github.io/GeoV2V/
summary: Novel view synthesis under trajectory changes is essential for autonomous driving simulation, yet existing methods struggle to generate consistent videos when extrapolating to unseen viewpoints such as lane shifts. Reconstruction-based approaches maintain geometric consistency but degrade in visual quality under large viewpoint changes, while reconstruct-then-restore methods often produce visually plausible frames yet suffer from geometric and temporal inconsistencies. We present GeoV2V, a geometry-grounded video-to-video diffusion framework that synthesizes temporally coherent driving videos along novel trajectories by integrating LiDAR and depth-derived geometric priors with full-video conditioning in the Wan 2.1 backbone. A key challenge in learning cross-lane transformations is the lack of synchronized multi-trajectory supervision in real-world datasets. To address this, we also introduce Para4D, a synthetic dataset capturing synchronized multi-lane driving videos within dynamic scenes, which provides explicit supervision for lane-shift generation and serves as a strong training prior for geometry-consistent view synthesis. Experiments on Waymo, nuScenes, and Para4D demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in visual quality, geometric consistency, and robustness to complex lighting dynamics under large trajectory shifts. Project page: https://xiyuche.github.io/GeoV2V/

title: Visual Scaffolding: Toward Native Multimodal Reasoning
summary: The success of chain-of-thought (CoT) in complex reasoning can be attributed to a textual scaffolding effect: explicit intermediate results can be examined, reused, and composed to support subsequent reasoning, much as scaffolding supports a building under construction. However, mainstream multimodal LLMs lack an equivalent scaffold for visual distinctions that are difficult to express in concise verbal descriptions. We therefore ask: Can native visual representations become first-class citizens alongside language, providing a visual scaffold for reasoning? We define native multimodal reasoning as reasoning in which native visual representations and language jointly carry reusable intermediate states. As a concrete implementation, the visual scaffolding mechanism we proposed lets the MLLM autonomously initiate a retrieval action at any reasoning step. A lightweight retriever selects native visual features, which are then incorporated directly into the evolving CoT and remain available to subsequent steps. To evaluate this mechanism under controlled visual demands, we introduce NMR-Bench, comprising Burden Counting and Path Tracing. With 88M added parameters (approximately 2%) on Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking, our model achieves 66.43% and 72.50% accuracy, respectively, surpassing the evaluated GPT-5.5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro baselines. Controlled interventions show that changing selected visual content affects task accuracy and can redirect subsequent visual selection even when intervening text is held fixed. These findings show that native visual states can function as intermediate reasoning material and point toward reusable scaffolds for additional modalities.

title: Persistent Representational Misalignment Induces Vision-Language Model Failures
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) fail at some tasks that are simple for humans---but why? We hypothesize that many such failures stem from VLMs' difficulties translating between vision and language representations, a misalignment the Platonic Representation Hypothesis predicts should disappear with scale. This paper is composed of two parts: in the first, we show that existing vision and language representations are linearly unalignable. This misalignment is an inherent property of the data and hence expected to persist regardless of either scale or the alignment's complexity. In the second, we demonstrate how this misalignment both leads to a predictably induced generalization failure and correlates with existing failure modes, where more representationally aligned VLM backbones accordingly exhibit fewer failures. Overall, these results imply representations will not become aligned simply given sufficient scale, providing evidence against a strong version of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

title: PanoDent-KD: From Generalist Knowledge Distillation to Cross-Dataset Specialist Detection and Embedded Deployment in Panoramic Radiographs
summary: Reliable panoramic-radiograph detection requires consistency across datasets with different class definitions and deployment software. We present PanoDent-KD, an auditable 1280-pixel YOLO26m pipeline linking a 12-class source generalist, feature-level knowledge distillation (KD), exact classifier-row transfer, teacher-free five-class specialization, and embedded deployment. A common training and evaluation pipeline compares three source-training arms across three seeds: a supervised baseline (B1), single-teacher KD (STKD), and multi-teacher KD (MTKD). Five shared classifier rows initialize nine OralXrays-9 specialists, while the backbone, FPN-PAN neck, and dual-detection-head topology are retained unchanged. On the 2,686-image test subset, all three arms achieve macro box F1 near 0.82. B1 achieves the highest three-seed arm-level mean macro box F1 (0.8239$\pm$0.0027) and $mAP_{50:95}$ (0.6130$\pm$0.0067). STKD seed 1, selected after development but before final testing, was used for deployment. Its Jetson Orin Nano Super FP16 TensorRT engine achieves 77.03-ms median and 80.86-ms P95 prediction-call latency, throughput of 12.90 images/s, and gross total-module energy of 1.39 J/image, with high numerical agreement between within-device PyTorch and TensorRT FP16 inference. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of an auditable, device-specific deployment workflow, but do not establish clinical validity or improved target-domain accuracy from KD.

title: GeoART: Geometry-Aware Refinement via Test-Time Scaling for Camera-Conditioned Video Diffusion
summary: Camera-conditioned video diffusion models often suffer from inaccurate camera control and geometric inconsisten- cies because camera constraints and estimated geometry are only weakly enforced during denoising. Existing reme- dies often require costly geometry-aware fine-tuning or ad- ditional 3D supervision. We introduce GeoART, a training- free self-refinement framework that improves camera con- trollability through geometry-aware test-time scaling. At selected denoising steps, GeoART generates multiple can- didates within the Predict-and-Perturb cycle and eval- uates them using a geometry prior, without directly modify- ing the denoising trajectory.
